title: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
summary: Classify text or images into labels you write at runtime: NLI entailment with hypothesis templates, embedding similarity to label descriptions, calibrated LLM prompting, and how to pick thresholds.
outcomes: Explain how NLI, embedding, and LLM scorers all turn labels into text and score them against the input
Compute single-label and multi-label scores from NLI logits and explain why multi_label changes the result
Compare T x N cross-encoder cost with T + N embedding cost and choose a family for a workload
Apply contextual calibration with a content-free input to remove an LLM's label bias
Choose multi-label thresholds from precision and recall on a labeled dev set

lessons.title: Classifying with labels chosen at inference time

blocks.md:
A normal text classifier is trained on a fixed label set. Its last layer has one output per label, so adding a label such as *refund request* means collecting labeled examples and retraining.

**Zero-shot classification** removes that step: you choose the labels at inference time, as plain text, and a model that was never trained on those labels scores each one. Yin, Hay, and Roth (2019) call the strict version *label-fully-unseen*: no labeled training data for any of the labels.

Every zero-shot classifier uses the same trick. First turn each label into text, either through a template (`This text is about {label}.`) or a longer description. Then score how well the input matches each label text with a model pretrained on some other, general task. Finally, apply a decision rule: pick the top label, or keep every label above a threshold.

This course covers three families of scorer, which differ in what the general task was:

- **NLI entailment**: a model trained to decide whether one sentence implies another.
- **Embedding similarity**: the cosine between an embedding of the input and an embedding of each label description.
- **LLM prompting**: ask a language model which label fits and read the probability of each label.

scenes.caption: The labels are just strings supplied at inference time. The first step is always to turn each one into a piece of text the pretrained model can read.
NLI scorer: the input is the premise and each filled-in template is a hypothesis. One forward pass per (text, label) pair.
Embedding scorer: the input and every label description are embedded separately, then compared with a cosine. Label embeddings can be computed once and cached.
LLM scorer: the labels go into a prompt and the model's probability for each label name becomes its score.
All three end the same way: one score per label, then argmax for single-label tasks or a threshold for multi-label tasks. Lesson 5 is about choosing that rule.

blocks.md:
You have already seen one instance of this recipe. In the CLIP course, the image is embedded and compared with text embeddings of prompts such as `A photo of a {label}.`, and the closest prompt wins. The CLIP paper reports that this single template improved ImageNet accuracy by 1.3% over bare class names, and that averaging 80 different templates per class gave a further 3.5%, almost 5% in total.

The ensemble is averaged in **embedding space**: each class gets one averaged text vector, so the classifier costs the same at inference as a single template. The paper also names the failure that templates fix: *polysemy*. ImageNet has both construction cranes and the bird, and in Oxford-IIIT Pets the class *boxer* means a dog breed, not an athlete.

In a zero-shot classifier, the label text plays the role of the trained weights. Changing a label's wording changes the classifier, so wording, templates, and descriptions are design decisions you test, not decoration.

Zero-shot does not mean zero data. You still need a small labeled set to compare templates, pick thresholds, and measure accuracy. The CLIP paper also reports a ceiling: on most of its datasets, zero-shot CLIP was 10% to 25% below a fully supervised linear classifier on the same features.

blocks.question: A support-ticket router uses an NLI zero-shot classifier with 6 labels. Product asks for a 7th label, refund request. What is the minimum change?
options: Add a 7th output unit to the model and fine-tune it on refund tickets
Append the string refund request to the label list, then re-check accuracy on a small labeled set
Retrain the NLI model on MNLI with refund examples added
Nothing: the model will start emitting the new label on its own
blocks.explain: The label set is an input at inference time, so adding a label is a one-line change. The model is never retrained. You should still re-check accuracy, because the new label competes with the existing ones and may steal their mass. The model cannot emit a label you did not pass in.

blocks.question: CLIP averages 80 prompt embeddings per class instead of averaging 80 sets of predicted probabilities. What does that buy at inference time?
options: Higher accuracy, because averaging probabilities is mathematically invalid
It removes the need for a temperature parameter
The ensemble costs the same as one prompt: one cached text vector per class, one image encoding per input
It lets CLIP output several labels per image
blocks.explain: Averaging in embedding space collapses the 80 prompts into one vector per class ahead of time. At inference, each image is still compared with exactly one vector per class, so the ensemble is free once the averages are cached. The paper gives exactly this reason.

lessons.title: NLI entailment: is the label a true statement about the text?

blocks.md:
**Natural language inference (NLI)** is a sentence-pair task. Given a *premise* and a *hypothesis*, a model predicts one of three labels: *entailment* (the premise implies the hypothesis), *neutral*, or *contradiction*. MNLI is a large public NLI dataset, and models fine-tuned on it are widely available.

Yin, Hay, and Roth observed that classification can be read as entailment: deciding whether a text is about sport is deciding whether the text entails the sentence *this text is about sport*. So the input text becomes the premise, and each label is slotted into a template to make a hypothesis. Their templates were `this text is about ?` for topics, `this text expresses ?` for emotions, and `The people there need ?` for disaster situations.

The model is a cross-encoder: it reads premise and hypothesis together as one sequence, so it can attend across both. The price is one forward pass per (text, label) pair. Classifying T texts against N labels costs T x N passes, and nothing can be cached across labels.

Our running example has 3 short texts and 4 labels (sports, technology, politics, complaint):

- **T1**: The battery died after two days and support never replied. (gold: complaint, technology)
- **T2**: Our team won the final in overtime last night. (gold: sports)
- **T3**: New tariffs will raise prices on imported phones. (gold: politics, technology)

The first gold label listed is the primary one. The logits below are illustrative numbers chosen for teaching, not outputs of a real model. Everything derived from them is computed exactly.

scenes.caption: Each cell is the entailment logit for premise = text, hypothesis = This example is {label}. That is 12 forward passes for 3 texts and 4 labels (illustrative values).
T1 has two high cells: technology (1.8) and complaint (2.4). Both hypotheses are plausibly true, which matters for how we turn logits into scores.
T2 is clear: only sports (3.1) is positive. Any sensible decision rule picks sports.
T3 is mostly politics (2.0), but technology (0.6) and complaint (0.3) are close to zero. These borderline cells are where the decision rule decides the outcome.

blocks.md: The Hugging Face `zero-shot-classification` pipeline implements this method. Its default `hypothesis_template` is `This example is {}.` and its default model is `facebook/bart-large-mnli`. The source code turns logits into scores in one of two ways, chosen by the `multi_label` flag:

blocks.caption: Left: softmax of the entailment logits across the N labels, so scores sum to 1. Right: for each label alone, softmax over just entailment and contradiction. The neutral logit is dropped in both.

blocks.prompt: T1 is both a technology problem and a complaint. With multi_label=False, will both labels get a high score?
blocks.reveal: No. The softmax across labels forces the scores to sum to 1, so the two true labels split the mass: complaint 0.638 and technology 0.350. With multi_label=True each label is judged on its own: complaint 0.985, technology 0.943. Use the first rule when exactly one label is correct, the second when several can be.

scenes.caption: T1, multi_label=False: softmax of entailment logits (-2.5, 1.8, -2.2, 2.4) across labels. Complaint wins with 0.638; technology gets 0.350 even though it is also true.

T1, multi_label=True: each label gets sigmoid(entailment minus contradiction). With contradiction logits -1.0 and -1.8, technology is sigmoid(2.8) = 0.943 and complaint sigmoid(4.2) = 0.985: both can be kept.
T3, multi_label=False: politics 0.695, technology 0.171, complaint 0.127. The argmax is right; the second true label looks weak.
T3, multi_label=True: politics 0.961, technology 0.646, complaint 0.574. Complaint is wrong but scores above 0.5, so a 0.5 threshold would add a false label. Lesson 5 picks the threshold.

blocks.code:
from transformers import pipeline

clf = pipeline("zero-shot-classification", model="facebook/bart-large-mnli")

out = clf(
    "The battery died after two days and support never replied.",
    candidate_labels=["sports", "technology", "politics", "complaint"],
    hypothesis_template="This text is about {}.",
    multi_label=True,  # score each label independently
)
print(out["labels"], out["scores"])  # labels sorted by score
blocks.caption: Pipeline call. The pipeline builds one (text, hypothesis) pair per label and runs them through the NLI model.

blocks.md:
Dropping neutral has a side effect. For T3 and technology, the full three-way softmax over (contradiction, neutral, entailment) logits (0.0, 1.0, 0.6) gives 0.180, 0.491, 0.329: the model mostly says *neutral*. The multi-label score ignores that and reports 0.646, the share of entailment among the two remaining options.

On evidence: Yin, Hay, and Roth tested BERT-base NLI models on unseen labels in 2019. For topics, plain label words in the hypothesis beat WordNet definitions by a wide margin (MNLI model: 43.4 versus 17.2 accuracy). The ensemble of their entailment models reached 45.7 on topics versus 35.7 for a word2vec similarity baseline, but a classifier trained on Wikipedia categories scored 52.1, so entailment was strong but not always best.

A multi_label score near 0.6 is not a 60% chance the label applies. It is the entailment share after throwing away the neutral mass, from a model trained on MNLI sentence pairs, not on your labels. Treat it as a ranking score and set thresholds on labeled data.

blocks.question: You run the NLI pipeline on 1,000 tickets with 50 candidate labels. How many NLI forward passes (one per sequence pair) does that take?
options: 50, one per label, cached across tickets
1,000, one per ticket
blocks.explain: The cross-encoder needs the premise and hypothesis together, so every (ticket, label) pair is its own forward pass: 1,000 x 50 = 50,000. Nothing about a label can be cached, because its representation depends on the ticket. This is the main cost of the NLI approach and grows linearly with the number of labels.

blocks.question: A teammate calls the pipeline with multi_label=False and keeps every label scoring above 0.5 as the ticket's tag set. What goes wrong?
options: At most one label can ever exceed 0.5, because the scores across labels sum to 1, so the system can never return two tags
Nothing; that is the intended way to do multi-label classification
Scores can exceed 1, so too many tags are returned
The neutral logit is added back in, inflating every score
blocks.explain: With multi_label=False the scores come from one softmax across labels and sum to 1, so two labels cannot both exceed 0.5. A ticket like T1 with two true labels gets 0.638 and 0.350 and loses technology. For several labels per input, use multi_label=True, which scores each label on its own.

blocks.md:
The second family uses a **bi-encoder**: one model maps any text to a vector, and texts are compared with cosine similarity. CLIP's zero-shot classifier is this design with an image encoder on one side. For text-only tasks, use a sentence-embedding model on both sides.

The classifier is: embed the input once, embed each label text once, compute the cosine to each label, and take the largest. The OpenAI Cookbook's zero-shot embedding example does exactly this for review sentiment, and reports that descriptive label texts such as `An Amazon review with a negative sentiment.` did better than the bare words *negative* and *positive*.

Because label embeddings do not depend on the input, they are computed once and cached. Classifying T texts against N labels costs T + N encoder passes instead of the T x N passes of NLI. For our example that is 3 + 4 = 7 passes versus 12, and adding another text costs one pass no matter how many labels there are. With thousands of labels, the label vectors can even sit in a vector index.

The matrix below shows illustrative cosines (not from a real model) for two versions of the labels: bare names, then one-sentence descriptions such as *A customer complaining about a product or service* and *News about government, laws, taxes or elections*.

blocks.title: Cosine to each label: bare names versus descriptions

scenes.caption: Bare label names. T1's best two cosines are 0.24 (technology) and 0.22 (complaint), a margin of 0.02: the argmax picks technology, and the ranking is fragile.
T3 with bare names: technology 0.27 beats politics 0.20. A one-word label like politics carries little meaning to match against tariffs and prices.
Switch to descriptions. T1 now has complaint 0.52 versus technology 0.33, and T3 has politics 0.44 versus technology 0.36. All three argmaxes match the primary gold label.
Note the scale moved too: bare-name cosines topped out at 0.31, description cosines reach 0.52. Any threshold tuned for one wording is meaningless for the other.

blocks.md: Cosines are not probabilities. They do not sum to 1, and their typical range depends on the embedding model. To get probability-like scores you can apply a softmax to the cosines multiplied by a scale $s$, which is what CLIP does with its learned temperature (clipped so logits are scaled by at most 100). The scale changes how confident the scores look, never which label ranks first.

blocks.title: Softmax confidence depends on an arbitrary scale

scenes.caption: T1 with descriptions: cosines 0.10, 0.33, 0.09, 0.52. At s=1 the softmax is nearly flat (complaint 0.319); by s=20 complaint is 0.978. Same cosines, very different confidence.
Shrink the margin to 0.02, as with bare label names. At s=20 complaint gets only 0.599 and at s=60 it gets 0.769: a larger scale can push a near tie toward false confidence.
Simplified: the other two cosines are held fixed. The lesson holds in general: the scale is a presentation knob, so pick thresholds from labeled data, not from how confident the softmax looks.

blocks.md:
For multi-label output, threshold the cosine per label. With the descriptions and a threshold of 0.30, T1 gets {technology, complaint}, T2 gets {sports}, and T3 gets {technology, politics}: all correct. With bare names, the same 0.30 threshold returns nothing at all for T1 and T3, because every bare-name cosine for those texts is below 0.28.

Embeddings measure topical similarity, which is not the same as inference. Yin, Hay, and Roth found word-vector similarity weak on emotion detection; their example is the text *when my brother was very late in arriving home from work*, whose gold label *fear* requires reasoning, not word overlap. NLI and LLM scorers handle that kind of label better.

Write label descriptions the way inputs are written. If the inputs are support tickets, *A customer complaining that a product stopped working* will sit closer to real complaints than the word *complaint*. Then re-tune any thresholds, since the cosine scale moves with the wording.

blocks.question: You rewrite all four label descriptions to be more specific. Which work must be redone?
options: Re-embed every input text and retrain the embedding model
Nothing; cosine similarity is unaffected by wording
Re-embed only the input texts
Re-embed the 4 label descriptions and re-tune the thresholds on labeled data
blocks.explain: Input embeddings do not depend on the labels, so they stay valid. The 4 label vectors must be recomputed, and because the cosine scale shifts with wording (bare names topped out at 0.31, descriptions at 0.52 in our example), any threshold has to be chosen again.

blocks.question: For T1 with descriptions, raising the softmax scale from 20 to 100 changes complaint's probability from 0.978 to about 1.0. What happens to accuracy?
options: It rises, because the model is more confident
It falls, because the model becomes overconfident
It does not change: scaling all cosines by the same factor keeps the ranking, so the argmax is identical
It depends on the embedding dimension
blocks.explain: Multiplying every cosine by the same positive number preserves their order, so the top label is unchanged for every input. Only the reported confidence changes, which is why softmax outputs from a hand-picked scale should not be read as calibrated probabilities.

lessons.title: Prompting an LLM and calibrating its label bias

blocks.md:
The third family asks a language model directly. The GPT-3 paper (Brown et al., 2020) defines the settings precisely. **Zero-shot**: the model gets only a natural-language instruction, no examples. **One-shot**: one demonstration. **Few-shot**: K demonstrations in the prompt, typically 10 to 100, as many as fit in the context window.

For binary classification the paper does not let the model write free text. It gives the options meaningful names (True or False rather than 0 or 1) and treats the task as multiple choice, comparing the model's likelihood of each option as the completion.

That is the key engineering point: **constrain the output to the label set**. Free generation can return *Tech-related issue* or a paragraph. There are two common ways to constrain it:

- **Score the label tokens.** Read the model's probability for each label name at the answer position and renormalize over just those labels. This is what Zhao et al. (2021) do, and it gives you a probability per label for free.
- **Constrained decoding.** Restrict generation to strings in the label set. The Outlines library, for example, accepts an output type like `Literal["Positive", "Negative", "Neutral"]` and guarantees the output is one of them.

The first is better when you want scores to threshold or calibrate; the second when an API only returns text.

blocks.code:
LABELS = ["sports", "technology", "politics", "complaint"]

prompt = (
    "Classify the text into one of: sports, technology, politics, complaint.\n"
    "Text: {text}\n"
    "Label:"
)

def label_probs(model, text):
    # probability of each label's first token at the answer position
    p = [model.next_token_prob(prompt.format(text=text), " " + lab) for lab in LABELS]
    total = sum(p)
    return [x / total for x in p]  # renormalize over the label set
blocks.caption: Label-token scoring, in sketch form. next_token_prob stands for whatever log-probability access your model gives you. If two labels share a first token, score whole label sequences instead.

blocks.md:
Zhao et al. found that these label probabilities are systematically shifted, and named three causes:

- **Majority label bias**: the model favors the label that appears most often among the prompt's examples.
- **Recency bias**: it favors labels that appear near the end of the prompt.
- **Common token bias**: it favors label words that are frequent in its pretraining data.

The effect is a constant shift. In one of their sentiment prompts, replacing the test input with the meaningless string `N/A` still produced 61.8% Positive. On a related prompt the paper shows that the default 0.5 threshold gave frequent false positives, while a threshold of 0.68 would have reached 94% validation accuracy: the information was there, the boundary was in the wrong place.

Their fix, **contextual calibration**, needs no labeled data. Run the same prompt with a *content-free* input in place of the text, read the label probabilities it produces, and divide them out. In the paper the content-free probabilities are averaged over three inputs: `N/A`, `[MASK]`, and the empty string.

blocks.caption: Zhao et al., Eq. 1. Dividing by the content-free probabilities makes the content-free input itself score uniform. Predictions are the argmax of W p + b.

blocks.title: Contextual calibration on the toy prompt

scenes.caption: Content-free input N/A, fed through the same prompt. With no text at all, the model already puts 0.46 on technology. All LLM probabilities in this example are illustrative.
Content-free input [MASK]: 0.08, 0.55, 0.13, 0.24.
Content-free input as the empty string: 0.10, 0.49, 0.16, 0.25.
Average of the three: p_cf = (0.10, 0.50, 0.15, 0.25). This vector is the prompt's bias, measured once and reused for every input.
T2 (the overtime final), raw: technology 0.48 narrowly beats sports 0.40. The bias toward technology flips a clear sports text.
T2 calibrated: divide by p_cf to get 4.0, 0.96, 0.333, 0.28, then renormalize: sports 0.718. The argmax is now correct.
T3 (tariffs), raw: technology 0.50 versus politics 0.40.
T3 calibrated: 0.40/0.15 = 2.667 beats 0.50/0.50 = 1.0, so politics wins with 0.637 after renormalizing.
T1 (battery), raw (0.03, 0.55, 0.04, 0.38) then calibrated: technology drops to 0.345 and complaint rises to 0.477. Raw accuracy on the primary label was 0 of 3; calibrated it is 3 of 3.

blocks.prompt: After calibration, what scores does the content-free input itself get?
blocks.reveal: Exactly uniform. Dividing p_cf by itself gives (1, 1, 1, 1), which renormalizes to 0.25 for each label. That is the design goal in Zhao et al.: an input that says nothing should favor no label, and whatever shift the prompt adds is removed from every real input too.

blocks.md: Two details. First, the bars show W p renormalized to sum to 1 for readability; the paper writes softmax(W p + b), which gives different numbers (T2 sports 0.911) but the same argmax, and the paper predicts with the argmax. Second, the bias is contextual: change the instruction, the examples, or their order, and p_cf must be measured again.

In the paper, contextual calibration improved average accuracy of GPT-3 and GPT-2 by up to 30.0% absolute across tasks and reduced the variance across prompt choices; with it, the 2.7B GPT-3 model sometimes beat the uncalibrated 175B model. The GPT-3 paper used a related correction on a few multiple-choice datasets (ARC, OpenBookQA, RACE): dividing each option's likelihood by its likelihood after a generic context such as `Answer: `. Both divide out how much the model likes an answer regardless of the question.

Constrain the LLM to the label set, read a probability per label, and divide by the probabilities a content-free input gets under the same prompt. Calibration fixes a constant shift; it cannot fix a model that does not understand the labels.

blocks.question: For a 4-label prompt, the content-free probabilities come out as (0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25). What does contextual calibration change?
options: It sharpens every prediction toward the top label
Nothing: W is 4 times the identity, which keeps the argmax and, after renormalizing, the probabilities
It flips the ranking of the top two labels
It sets every prediction to uniform
blocks.explain: W = diag(1/0.25) = 4I, which scales every label equally. The argmax cannot change and renormalized probabilities are unchanged. Calibration only matters when the prompt has a bias, which is exactly when p_cf is not uniform.

blocks.question: A team measured p_cf with a zero-shot prompt, then switched to an 8-shot prompt with more technology examples and kept the old p_cf. What is the bug?
options: None; p_cf depends only on the model weights
p_cf should have been measured on the test set
Calibration only applies to zero-shot prompts
The bias is contextual: new examples change majority and recency bias, so p_cf must be re-measured with the new prompt
blocks.explain: Zhao et al. stress that the error is contextual: a different choice, order, or format of examples changes the content-free prediction. Adding technology examples would likely push the model further toward technology, which the stale p_cf does not account for.

lessons.title: Evaluating zero-shot classifiers and choosing thresholds

blocks.md:
Every choice in the earlier lessons (template, label wording, scoring rule, scale, threshold) was a decision you could only judge on labeled examples. So in practice zero-shot classification still needs a small labeled **development set**. It is used for evaluation and for a handful of choices, not for training weights.

For single-label tasks, report accuracy, or a label-weighted F1 when classes are unbalanced; Yin, Hay, and Roth used accuracy for topics and label-weighted F1 for emotions and situations. For multi-label tasks, every (text, label) pair is a yes/no decision, scored with precision and recall.

blocks.caption: TP: predicted and true. FP: predicted but not true. FN: true but missed. Micro-averaging counts these over all (text, label) pairs.

blocks.md: Take the multi-label NLI scores from lesson 2: 3 texts x 4 labels = 12 decisions, 5 of them truly positive. A label is predicted when its score is at least the threshold. Watch which cells flip as the threshold rises.

blocks.title: Twelve label decisions at four thresholds

scenes.caption: Columns are sports, technology, politics, complaint; scores are the multi_label=True NLI scores. The 5 true labels are T1 technology and complaint, T2 sports, T3 technology and politics.
Threshold 0.5: all 5 true labels are kept (green), but T3 complaint at 0.574 is a false positive (red). TP 5, FP 1, FN 0.
Threshold 0.6: the false positive drops out and nothing true is lost. TP 5, FP 0, FN 0 on this tiny set.
Threshold 0.7: T3 technology at 0.646 is now missed (purple marks a false negative). TP 4, FN 1.
Threshold 0.95: T1 technology (0.943) is also lost. Only the most confident label per text survives. TP 3, FN 2.

blocks.title: Precision, recall and F1 as the threshold rises

scenes.caption: Threshold 0.5: precision 5/6 = 0.833, recall 1.0, F1 0.909.
Threshold 0.6: precision 1.0, recall 1.0, F1 1.0 on these 12 decisions.
Threshold 0.7: precision stays 1.0 but recall falls to 4/5 = 0.8, F1 0.889.
Threshold 0.95: recall 3/5 = 0.6, F1 0.75. Raising the threshold trades recall for precision; where to stop depends on which error costs more.

blocks.md: The perfect F1 at 0.6 comes from 12 decisions on 3 hand-picked texts. A threshold tuned on so few examples is overfit. Use hundreds of labeled examples, and keep a separate test split to report the final number.

Practical rules for choosing thresholds:

- **Sweep, then pick by the cost of errors.** scikit-learn's `precision_recall_curve` returns precision and recall at every distinct score, so you can choose, for example, the lowest threshold with precision of at least 0.95 when a wrong tag is expensive.
- **Use per-label thresholds.** Scores are not comparable across labels, because each label has its own hypothesis or description. A label with vague wording may need a different cut.
- **Re-tune when anything upstream changes**: the model, the template, the label wording, or the prompt.
- **Plan for none of the above.** A softmax across labels always picks something. Either threshold the top score and abstain below it, or use independent scores and return nothing when no label passes.

Choosing a family, with T texts and N labels:

- **NLI cross-encoder**: T x N passes, nothing cached. Good when labels are statements that need inference (emotions, needs), with a moderate number of labels.
- **Embeddings**: T + N passes, label vectors cached; scales to thousands of labels. Weaker when the label requires reasoning rather than topical similarity.
- **LLM prompt**: one call per text with all labels in the prompt, so it is flexible (instructions, definitions, edge cases) but each call is the most expensive. Constrain outputs and calibrate.

Once labeled data accumulates, consider training a small classifier. The CLIP paper reports that on ImageNet zero-shot CLIP matched a linear classifier trained with 16 examples per class on the same features: zero-shot is a strong start, not a ceiling.

Zero-shot replaces training data with design choices. Make those choices on a labeled dev set: compare templates or descriptions, pick argmax or per-label thresholds by the cost of errors, and re-check whenever the labels change.

blocks.question: An auto-tagger publishes tags without human review, and a wrong tag is costly while a missing tag is cheap. How should you set the threshold?
options: Use 0.5, since the scores are probabilities
Pick the threshold that maximizes recall
Use multi_label=False and always take the top label
On a labeled dev set, pick the lowest threshold that reaches the precision target, then confirm on a held-out test split
blocks.explain: When false positives are expensive, you constrain precision and take as much recall as that allows. 0.5 has no special meaning for these scores (T3 complaint scored 0.574 and was wrong). Always taking the top label guarantees a tag even when none applies.

blocks.question: A classifier must handle inputs that match none of 20 labels. It uses NLI with multi_label=False and returns the argmax. What happens on an off-topic input?
options: It returns a label anyway, because the softmax across labels always sums to 1 and some label must win
It returns an empty list
It raises an error because no hypothesis is entailed
It returns all 20 labels with score 0.05
blocks.explain: A softmax across labels forces a distribution, so the argmax always names a label, even for an input that entails none of them. To support none of the above, threshold the top score and abstain, or use independent per-label scores and return nothing when none pass.

blocks.question: You have 200,000 product descriptions and 5,000 category labels, and need one pass over them tonight. Which family fits the budget best?
options: NLI cross-encoder, because it is the most accurate
Embedding similarity: 205,000 encoder passes with cached label vectors, versus a billion pairs for NLI
An LLM call per (description, label) pair
Contextual calibration alone
blocks.explain: NLI needs one pass per pair: 200,000 x 5,000 = 1 billion. Embeddings need one pass per description plus one per label, 205,000 in total, and label vectors can sit in a vector index for fast lookup. You can still rerank the top few candidates per item with a slower scorer.
